title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
hook: a snake's shed skin lies on a rock, perfect and empty. Shankara borrows that image for the one who knows
carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the fourth line: freedom isn't made, so what frees is knowing. Did you catch yourself on tiptoe, trying to earn what you had? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

On a warm rock beside a hiking trail lies a snake's skin. Whole. Every scale is printed on it, even the shape of the eyes. Hikers stop and lean in, a little thrilled and a little nervous. But there's nothing to be nervous about. The snake is long gone. What's left keeps the exact shape of a living thing, and nobody lives in it anymore. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad uses that picture for the body of someone who has come to know. Shankara reaches for it near the end of his comment on the fourth line. Today we close our time with these four opening lines, and with the word jnana.
screen: `A SKIN ON A WARM ROCK.` → `THE SHAPE, AND NOBODY IN IT.` → `THE LAST DAY ON FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: Start with the four lines themselves, laid end to end. One: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. Two: that from which this world comes, stays, and goes. Three: because of being the source of scripture. Four: but that, because the texts are connected in it. A wish, a pointer, a source, a harmony. Some readers treat these four lines as the whole case in miniature. Now the image. The Upanishad says: as a snake's cast-off skin lies on an anthill, lifeless, thrown away, so lies this body. Shankara uses it to describe the one who knows. Being embodied, he says, comes from the old mix-up, the I taken for the body, the this taken for the I. When knowing removes the mix-up, the body doesn't vanish. It goes on walking, eating, getting tired. But it's no longer taken for the self. Like the skin on the rock, it keeps its shape, and nobody is trapped inside it. Then Shankara adds a test that's hard to forget. Someone who has truly understood, he says, no longer lives in the turning world the way they did before. And someone who still lives in it exactly as before hasn't understood yet. Jnana, for him, isn't a theory you hold. It's a knowing that changes where you stand. That was the gift of these days: the mix-up, the puzzle of the known and the unknown, the post in the fog, a line read twice, freedom that isn't made, and now the skin on the rock. Other schools read these lines differently. We let Shankara speak.
screen: `A WISH, A POINTER, A SOURCE, A HARMONY.` · `THE SNAKE'S CAST-OFF SKIN.` · `THE BODY NO LONGER TAKEN FOR THE SELF.` · `KNOWING CHANGES WHERE YOU STAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the body be held without holding it. Settle, and feel the whole body sitting, from the soles of the feet to the top of the head. Let it be heavy. Let the chair or the floor carry it. Feel the places where it touches down: heels, hands, the back of the legs. You don't need to push the body away. Just let it rest, like something set down. If you pray, you can offer the body's weight. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that removes the mix-up and changes where you stand, as a snake leaves its skin behind. Today's word.

Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Today, when you set something heavy down, let it remind you of the skin on the rock. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers often read the Brahma Sutra's opening lines with students as a summary of the whole work, together with Shankara's commentary on them.

match.prompt: four lines, four pieces — tap the pairs.
pairs: that from which this world comes

myth: for Shankara, the body vanishes when someone comes to know
it goes on, like the skin on the rock, but it's no longer taken for the self.
the snake's cast-off skin image comes from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
Shankara borrows it near the end of his comment on the fourth line.
Shankara says someone can understand and live exactly as before
he says whoever still lives in the turning world as before hasn't understood yet.

fork.setup: you've read the four opening lines with Shankara. someone asks: so has the knower left their body behind? what does he answer?
options: the body goes on, but it isn't taken for the self.
fork.reveal: like a snake's cast-off skin: the shape remains, and nobody is trapped inside it.

original.note: Sanskrit: knowing; on a path of knowing, the insight that frees.

trapdoor: what you thought: jnana is a set of correct ideas about God.
what it means: for Shankara, jnana removes the mix-up of the I and the body, and changes how a person lives.
what a scholar hears: the close of Shankara on 1.1.4, citing Brihadaranyaka 4.4.7, the slough of a snake, for the knower as bodiless while living.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.4, closing section (embodiment rooted in false knowledge; the knower bodiless even while living; one who has understood does not belong to the round of rebirth as before)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.7 (as the slough of a snake lies on an anthill, dead and cast away, so lies this body)

notes: Last of six days on Shankara's commentary on 1.1.1–1.1.4. Recap: preface (1232), known/unknown (1233), post in the fog (1234), two readings of 1.1.3 (1235), freedom not produced (1236), the snake's slough (1237).

Confirm that Shankara cites Brihadaranyaka 4.4.7 (the snake's slough) in the closing part of his comment on 1.1.4, and the paraphrase that one who has understood does not belong to the transmigratory world as before, while one who still does has not understood.
'Some readers treat these four lines as the whole case in miniature' is a soft summary of the tradition of treating them as the chatuh-sutri; confirm or cut.
The hiking-trail framing is modern; the Upanishad sets the skin on an anthill, as the teach says.
Editor pass: practice no longer ends on 'notice the noticing itself' (repeated 1229, 1232 and 1233); it now rests on where the body touches down.
